'''Ralph Saul Phillips''' (23 June 1913 – 23 November 1998) was an American mathematician and academic known for his contributions to [[functional analysis]], [[scattering theory]], and [[servomechanism]]s. He served as a professor of mathematics at [[Stanford University]]. He made major contributions to acoustical scattering theory in collaboration with [[Peter Lax]], proving remarkable results on local energy decay and the connections between poles of the [[S-matrix|scattering matrix]] and the analytic properties of the [[Resolvent formalism|resolvent]]. With Lax, he coauthored the widely referred book on [[scattering theory]] titled ''Scattering Theory for Automorphic Functions''. Phillips received the 1997 [[Leroy P. Steele Prize]] for Lifetime Achievement.<ref name="ams_steel">{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199703/comm-steele.pdf|title=1997 Steele Prizes|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=26 June 2010}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Phillips was born in [[Oakland, California|Oakland]] on 23 June 1913. He received his bachelor's degree from the [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California]] at [[Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1935 and his Ph.D. from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1939 under the direction of Theophil H. Hildebrandt.<ref name="math"/>

From 1939 until 1942 he was a member of the Institute for Advanced Study in [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]], an instructor at the [[University of Washington]], and an instructor at [[Harvard University]]. It was at the University of Washington he met his future wife, Jean.<ref name="ams">{{cite journal
 | last = Sarnak | first = Peter | author-link = Peter Sarnak
 | issue = 5
 | journal = Notices of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1750667
 | pages = 561–563
 | title = Ralph Phillips (1913–1998)
 | url = https://www.ams.org/notices/200005/mem-phillips.pdf
 | volume = 47
 | year = 2000}}</ref> During the war he led a research group at the Radiation Laboratory at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], the facility where much of the theoretical and practical work on radar technology was done. This work led to his book Theory of Servomechanisms,<ref>{{cite book|editor1=H. M. James|editor2=N. B. Nichols|editor3=R. S. Phillips|title=Theory of Servomechanisms|year=1947|publisher=McGraw-Hill|url=http://cer.ucsd.edu/~james/notes/MIT%20OpenCourseWare/MIT%20Radiation%20Lab/PREF25.PDF|access-date=2010-06-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100705063902/http://cer.ucsd.edu/~james/notes/MIT%20OpenCourseWare/MIT%20Radiation%20Lab/PREF25.PDF|archive-date=2010-07-05|url-status=dead}}</ref> which for many years was the standard text in the subject. After the war he returned to mathematics, joining as an assistant professor at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]]. He moved to the [[University of Southern California]] the next year and returned to UCLA in 1958. In 1960 he joined [[Stanford University]] and remained there until his death in 1998. He was the Robert Grimmett Professor of mathematics at Stanford. Philips's work (with [[Alexander Lubotzky|A. Lubotzky]] and [[Peter Sarnak|P. Sarnak]]) on [[Ramanujan graphs]] had a huge impact on [[combinatorics]] and [[computer science]].
